module_title: Nutrition for GERD and Acid Reflux
review_status: AI draft - scientific, clinical, and editorial review required
content: Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD) is a chronic condition where stomach acid or bile flows back into the esophagus, causing symptoms such as heartburn and regurgitation. This reflux occurs because of malfunctioning mechanisms including a weak lower esophageal sphincter, delayed gastric emptying, and increased intra-abdominal pressure. Nutrition plays a critical role in managing GERD, as certain dietary habits and foods can exacerbate or alleviate symptoms. Key nutritional factors include meal size and timing; smaller, more frequent meals may reduce reflux episodes by minimizing gastric distension, while avoiding late meals can prevent nighttime reflux. Dietary triggers vary but commonly include fatty foods, spicy foods, caffeine, chocolate, and acidic items like citrus fruits and tomatoes. Weight management is important because excess body weight increases pressure on the abdomen, promoting reflux. Practical nutrition strategies incorporate identifying individual triggers, adjusting meal patterns, and maintaining a healthy weight. However, limitations in current evidence include variability in individual responses and a lack of consensus on some dietary recommendations. Complementary lifestyle measures such as elevating the head of the bed and avoiding tobacco also support symptom control. Understanding these nutritional factors offers patients actionable tools alongside medical management to improve quality of life in GERD. Related concepts include the physiology of the lower esophageal sphincter, the role of gastric emptying, and pharmacologic therapies used in treatment.

content: GERD occurs when the lower esophageal sphincter (LES) fails to close properly, allowing stomach acid to flow back into the esophagus. This acid reflux can cause heartburn, chest discomfort, and regurgitation. Contributing factors include a weakened LES, hiatal hernia, obesity, and delayed stomach emptying. Recognizing symptoms early helps in timely management.

chunk_title: Common Dietary Triggers of Acid Reflux
content: Several foods are known to exacerbate acid reflux symptoms. These include fatty and fried foods, spicy dishes, chocolate, caffeine, carbonated beverages, citrus fruits, and tomatoes. Not all individuals react the same way, so identifying personal trigger foods through observation or elimination diets is useful.

chunk_title: Meal Size and Frequency: Impact on GERD
content: Large meals cause the stomach to stretch and increase gastric pressure, promoting reflux. Consuming smaller, more frequent meals reduces gastric distension and may alleviate symptoms. Avoiding overeating and spacing meals appropriately can contribute to better reflux control.

chunk_title: Timing of Meals and Nighttime Symptoms
content: Eating close to bedtime can worsen GERD symptoms by allowing acid reflux when lying down. It is recommended to have the last meal at least 2–3 hours before lying down or sleeping. Elevating the head during sleep can also reduce nighttime reflux.

chunk_title: The Role of Body Weight in GERD
content: Excess body weight, especially abdominal obesity, increases intra-abdominal pressure and the likelihood of reflux episodes. Weight reduction through diet and exercise has been shown to improve GERD symptoms. Maintaining a healthy weight is a key strategy in managing reflux.

content: Beyond avoiding triggers, some research supports diets rich in fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and lean proteins to improve GERD symptoms. The Mediterranean diet, for example, has emerging evidence suggesting benefit. However, more studies are needed to establish definitive dietary patterns for GERD.
